headline: Highest risk is medium prompt-injection and data leakage via shared project-directory workflows; no direct evidence of a dangerous default bridge, but gpt-engineer’s file-writing and Taipy’s data-engineering role create plausible…

A_prompt_injection.rationale: gpt-engineer writes files in a per-project directory and can execute generated code; Taipy is a data-engineering tool with no documented isolation or provenance controls. If Taipy ingests files from the shared project directory, attacker-controlled content from gpt-engineer can be treated as instructions. The interaction is plausible but not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes to medium.
conditions: IF Taipy reads prompts or config from the shared project directory without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF gpt-engineer writes untrusted content that Taipy later parses as instructions, the pathway is active.
mitigations: Separate the agents into different directories.
Disable automatic parsing of generated files by Taipy.
Add a manual review step before Taipy consumes gpt-engineer outputs.
Use read-only mounts for Taipy inputs where possible.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between producer and consumer.

B_data_leakage.rationale: gpt-engineer touches generated source code and handles OPENAI_API_KEY, while Taipy is a data-engineering tool with no stated data-handling limits. Because gpt-engineer shares state via the project directory and has broad network egress, sensitive files in that workspace could flow into either agent’s outputs or external API calls. The shared-workspace leakage path is plausible, though not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF sensitive files are placed in the shared project directory, both agents can access them.
IF Taipy processes those files and emits them into logs or outputs, leakage occurs.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared project directory.
Use separate workspaces for code and data.
Redact sensitive fields before either agent reads them.
Restrict outbound network access for the workspace.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent access controls on shared files.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: gpt-engineer has filesystem write, shell, subprocess, and broad network egress; Taipy is a data-engineering tool with no concurrency or locking details. Even though Taipy’s write scope is undocumented, the pair can still conflict on shared mutable project files if both operate in the same directory. Because the overlap is plausible but not fully specified, medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same project directory, file clobbering can occur.
IF Taipy mutates shared artifacts without locks, concurrent updates can race.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working directory.
Serialize writes with a simple operator-managed lock file.
Avoid concurrent runs on the same project.
Snapshot the workspace before each agent runs.
requires-engineering: add transactional locking around shared artifacts.

D_cascading_error.rationale: gpt-engineer produces generated code and writes files, while Taipy is a data-engineering/automation tool that may consume upstream artifacts. If Taipy treats gpt-engineer output as authoritative without verification, errors can cascade into downstream data workflows. No direct evidence shows automatic trust, so medium reflects a plausible default-path failure rather than a proven one.
conditions: IF Taipy consumes gpt-engineer-generated files without validation, downstream errors can propagate.
IF generated code is executed or scheduled by Taipy, faulty assumptions can cascade.
mitigations: Require human review before Taipy uses generated artifacts.
Add schema and unit checks on gpt-engineer outputs.
Run Taipy in a dry-run mode first.
Keep execution separate from generation.
requires-engineering: implement validation gates between the agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Both agents are open-source and the profiles do not show a residency, certification, or retention mismatch. gpt-engineer handles an OPENAI_API_KEY and broad network egress, but Taipy has network egress none and no data classes listed. With no documented compliance conflict, only a small residual risk remains from unspecified deployment choices.
conditions: IF deployment places regulated data into gpt-engineer’s external model calls, compliance obligations may change.
IF Taipy is configured to store regulated data with different retention rules than gpt-engineer, a mismatch can arise.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of model prompts.
Document retention settings for both agents.
Review whether external API calls are allowed for the data class.
Use separate storage policies for code and data.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for regulated datasets.
